keys.description: shared internal secret the /internal/validate endpoint requires (fail-closed guard, main.py). Unset, gateway's validation hop 503s and every API-key check fails — so the boot refuses instead of coming up green and rejecting every call (the 2026-04-23 failure shape, #526). The same value gates /internal/bootstrap-admin and /internal/users/by-email, so a published placeholder is refused outright (F95).

keys.default: (unset — the admin surface then answers 500 'Admin authentication is not configured')
keys.description: admin bearer for the privileged admin surface (main.py:_admin_token → os.getenv, NO code default; every /admin route and the key-minting surface behind it). It read 'changeme' here, which described the deploy surfaces rather than the code — and that is exactly what a published default is: this token MINTS AN API KEY FOR ANY USER, so a stack left on the literal hands the whole account plane to anyone who read the repository. Same refusal INTERNAL_API_SECRET got in F95, for a strictly larger blast radius (A19).

bounded initial-DB-connect retry: max attempts before failing loud. On a cold start where Postgres DNS isn't resolvable yet, the boot retries the first connect instead of exit(3)-ing into the k8s restart loop (#901). After this many attempts it re-raises.
bounded initial-DB-connect retry: base backoff seconds (capped-exponential: base×2^(n-1), clamped to DB_CONNECT_MAX_DELAY). #901.
bounded initial-DB-connect retry: max backoff seconds per attempt (the exponential is clamped here). #901.

flows' intake, told that a person finished onboarding. IDENTITY TELLS FLOWS; IT DOES NOT ASK IT — the publish is best-effort, bounded at 2s and swallowed, so a deployment with no flows domain onboards people exactly as one with a flows domain does, and so does one where flows is simply down. Unset is therefore not a degraded state, it is a profile. The fact itself is stamped on the person in the same transaction as the account, so the record survives a publish that never lands (app/events.py, app/main.py POST /admin/users). Spelled bare FLOWS_API_URL until F208 — the only one of the three flows publishers not carrying the VEXA_ prefix this repo uses for its own keys; app/events.py still reads that name for one release, with a boot warning, so an unmigrated deployment keeps publishing.

operator key for the same edge, sent as X-Flows-Operator-Key (flows' POST /events is authenticated). The header was spelled X-Flows-Admin-Key until #1486 and flows still accepts that name for one release; admin-api sends only the new one. Declared as part of the edge rather than beside it: a publish target without its credential is a publish that always 401s, and the pair is what makes the edge real. Unset alongside an unset URL is the no-flows profile; unset with a URL set is a deployment whose facts are being refused, which is why both are visible on one declaration.

Stripe's account secret key (sk_...), bearer-authenticates every REST call `billing/stripe_gateway.StripeClient` makes — create customer, create checkout/portal session, and the webhook handler's re-read of a subscription's current state. Unset ⇒ POST /billing/checkout, POST /billing/portal and POST /billing/webhook all answer a typed 503 naming the missing key(s); the rest of admin-api is unaffected (DB-73).

the whsec_... signing secret POST /billing/webhook verifies the Stripe-Signature header against (HMAC-SHA256 over "{t}.{raw_body}", constant-time compare, 300s timestamp tolerance — billing/stripe_gateway.verify_signature). One per registered Stripe webhook endpoint; a deployment that rotates it sends the payload signed under both the old and new secret for a transition window, and verify_signature checks every v1 entry against the ONE secret this key holds — set the new value only after the old endpoint is retired, or run two endpoints during rotation.

where Stripe Checkout redirects after a successful subscription purchase (the dashboard's billing page, e.g. https://app.example.com/settings/billing?checkout=success). Never invented — POST /billing/checkout passes it to Stripe verbatim.
where Stripe Checkout redirects when the person abandons the purchase (e.g. https://app.example.com/settings/billing?checkout=cancelled).
where the Stripe Customer Portal (card changes, cancellation, invoices) returns the person to (e.g. https://app.example.com/settings/billing).

the OAuth client id (google_oauth.py) DB-30's Google Calendar connect flow presents to Google — a DIFFERENT OAuth client than the dashboard's own sign-in GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID (a different consent: read-only calendar access vs. 'sign in with Google'). ONE Google Cloud OAuth client MAY serve both purposes if both redirect URIs are registered on it (see docs/docs/how-to/calendar-sync.mdx for the exact console steps) — but the two env keys must never be conflated in code, because calendar_readonly consent must never be silently granted by a sign-in flow the user did not see as a calendar request.

the OAuth client secret paired with GOOGLE_CALENDAR_CLIENT_ID. Lives ONLY in admin-api (google_oauth.py's code/refresh-token exchange) — never sent to, or readable by, the dashboard or any other service.

the dashboard's public OAuth callback page (DB-31), e.g. https://dashboard.vexa.ai/calendar/google/callback — MUST exactly match a redirect URI registered on the Google Cloud OAuth client (GOOGLE_CALENDAR_CLIENT_ID), or Google refuses the consent screen with redirect_uri_mismatch. Never guessed from another env var: DB-31's callback page relays {code, state} to POST /user/calendars/google/exchange through the dashboard's own proxy, and this is the exact address that page must live at.

the AES-256-GCM master key token_cipher.py encrypts the Google refresh token with (see token_cipher.py's module docstring for the construction). Standard base64 of exactly 32 raw bytes — generate with `python -c "import os,base64;print(base64.b64encode(os.urandom(32)).decode())"`. Without it the Google OAuth routes answer their capability-gated 503 rather than ever writing a refresh token to users.data unencrypted; rotating it makes every previously-stored Google connection's stored blob undecryptable, surfacing as reconnect_needed on next sync (the same visible state a revoked Google grant produces) rather than a silent failure.
